So,mu official þÿ Correspondencerespecting emigration from þÿCanton lias been laid before Parliament, which shows the abominable character of the coolie trade carried on at. Canton and Whampoa. Forc'gn vessels arriving there to engage and einbaik emigrant labourers have sought the assistance of native brockers, who, .in their turn, have employed ciimps (also Chinese) to collect coolies for them. 30 dollars ahead or more were being paid last year for coolies delivered on hoard ; arrived at the Havnnnah, the þÿ"Contracts could be sold at 400 dollars a bead. An iniqnitious system was thus created, which grew until not on men were ly inveigled on board receiving ships on false pretexts, such as promises of work, but force also was Used, and no man could leave his house in open day without danger of being hustled, under false pretence of debt or delinquency, and carried ofl by the crimps to be put on board ships and taken to sea, never again to be heard of. Chinese women have been employed. For instance þÿ a woman with a child on her back caused the þÿchild bonnet s to fall as she passed two men ; on
offered them some cakes for their civility ; these were eaten, and, being drugged, the men sat down stupified ; the þÿwomau s confederates then I the slave trade, once so vigorously carried on

S: fu M O I.J ¥ I. S came up, offered to carry the two men home, but lodged them in a receiving-ship instead. A few months ago. in consequence of exposure, above 100 coolies were rescued from receiving vessels, and described tbe way in which t hey were kidnapped, and got into boats, where they were intimidated or tortured, in order to wring irom them, when taken on board the receivingship, a nominal cousent to an eight þÿyears engagement in Cuba, deception being also practised to make them believe that their shipment had the sanction of the authorities. The torture consists in tying a man up by the thumbs and toes, and in other painful positions, and heating him; applying a lighted stick to the j feet, binding tbe bands together, and then driving a wedge in between them, ducking him in tbe water, and keeping him half drowned ; and it is alleged that some who attempted to escape by swimming were harpooned by their countrymen like fish. If in the receiving-ship they would not give their consent to go, they were taken back into the Chinese boat for a renewal of the. torture, The system became so terrible last year that a popular rising was apprehended. Then the Governor ot Canton tried severe measures. Convicted crimps were beheaded (IS in one day), and t be woman who had been the instrument of kidnappers was subjected by the authorities to mutilations which it would be shocking to describe Several kidnappers, also, were killed by the mob with a vindictive cruelly to which there was too much

provocation. In tlnse circumstances Laou, acting Goveiuoi -Gr tie nil of the Two Kwangs, consented to endeavour to put an end to this "sale of þÿpigs, as it is called, by substituting for it a legalised system of lice , migration. At He close ot last year Mr .J. G Austin, authorised by the British government to conduct emigration to our West Indian colonies, opened an emigration bouse at Canton with the sanction of the Chinese authorities, under arrangements that tender coercion impossible, securing to tbe emigrants when arrived in the colony woik as agricultural labourers for monthly wages, with bouse, garden ground, and unions, or task worth work without rations, if they prefer it, the only condition being that tin y shall serve for five yea is or repay their passage money, or part ol it, according to the time not served ; if their families also go, they are taken free of charge, and have an allowance for extra comforts on the passage. By' the middle of March last, Mr. Austin had despatched to British Guiana 1,307 men, 299 women, and 108 children, the ships having none hut voluntary emigrants on board, and quitting Canton amid cheers and fire- works. One of the ships took the inhabitants of an entire village, who left owing to a feud with another and larger village, and the consequent destruction of growing crops. The French soon followed our example, and opt tied also their emigration at Canton; and an Americau agent for a Cuba bouse has done, or is about to do. the

same. The Imperial Commissioner Ao. however, still treats emigration as altogether prohibited, and it is feared that in so doing represents faithfully the sentiments ol the Court of þÿl ekin. The correspondences close with an important despatch from Lord John Bussell to Earl Cowley, a similar letter being addressed to Mr. Edwards, Lord Lyons, and Sir A. Magenis. Under these cii cutnstances her þÿMajesty s Government appeal to the nations of Christendom to endeavour, in obedience to the dictates of humanity and religion, to efface, by a fiual their picking it up she expressed her thanks and j effort, the stain which the slave trade inflicts on the Christian name Brazil has set a noble example of perseverance in tbe suppression to of

her shores ; and what the Brazilian Government, in the face of great difficulties, has successfully accomplished, may is be now plished elsewhere. Cuba equally accom almost the only place in the globe by whicli Her the slave trade is maintained. and for which þÿMajesty s Government have a treaty with Spain ot the year 1835, by which the Spanish Crown undertook to abolish the slave trade, and accepted a sum of £400,000 to enable it the more easily to do so. Her Majesty' Government are well aware that the price of sugar and the demand j for labour afford the slave trader profits which j enable hint to corrupt the authorities whose duty it is to thwart and defeat his criminal enterprises. It appears to her þÿMajesty Govern- s ment that some remedy for this state of things might be found in an improvement of the laws of the United States respecting the equipment of slave ships, and in the increased employment of cruisers in the waters surrounding Cuba by Spain, Great Britain, and the United States, and in the enactment by Spain of a law enforcing the registration of slaves in Cuba, and inflicting severe penalties upon the proprietors of estates within which newly imported slaves a>e found. But no doubt tbe difficulties of suppressing the slave trade arise mainly from the demand which exists in Cuba and similar count) ies for labourers suited to a hot climate ; and if this demand eould lie lawfully supplied, the incentives to engage in an illegal traffic in African labourers would be greatly diminished,

and the price of a slave might be enhanced far beyond that of a free labourer. This supply Her þÿMajesty s Government confidently believe may be obtained from China. Moreover, under the regulations which have been introduced by the agent in China of Her þÿMajesty Government s iu conjunction with the Chinese and the allied authorities at Canton, it has been found practicable to induce whole families of Chinese to emigrate. A considerable number of such families have emigrated to Dcmerara, and there is every reason to hope that with time and care the prejudices which have hitherto prevented Chinese women from emigrating may be entirely overcome. Ozanatn, bis experiments having been made upon animals so much under the influence of chlo-oform that respiration had become very feeble, the beating of the heart almost imperceptible, and death imminent. From the London Times , September 14. ITALY. It is probable that the course of events in Italy has bewildered even those most intimately concerned iu the promotion of the catastiophe. Nobody could have anticipated þÿGaribaldi s career of conquest, or foreseen the character of that astonishing revolution which is now resolving organized States into the most primitive elements of political community. History itself scarcely offers a parallel to the spectacle at this moment presented by Southern Italy. To find a precedent for such a pic me we must trace back the stream i f time up u> the decay of the Homan Empire, when the w hole of the lace iif Europe was changed, trod its population gravitated to new centres of power. Scenes apparently similar were mac e l, it is true, during the wars of the French E volution, and especially towards the close of that eventful period, but revolution bad been then denies icated, and the Governments sui v, rod to make way for others were themselves only a few years old. Perhaps the clo- st parallel of all would be found in the state of affairs which þÿNapoleon s return from Elba produced iu France ; but then Napoleon had ipiitt, d France only 10 months before, and lie reappeared as the restorer of an Empire to which, not withstanding the sufferings it had cost them, a large portion of the French people looked with affection and pride. When, again, the abdication of Louis Philippe brought the downfall of lbs dynasty, the phenomenon caused hut little surprise, for the deposed monarch was hut the li st

of his line, and the same generation which witnessed his flight could remember his accession But, no considerations of this kind present themselves to explain t lie revolutions now oi cm ring in Italy. Rome and Naples ate the capitals of ancient States, ruled by Governments of ancient standing, and owned by legitimate Sovereigns. Francis II is the representative of a monarchy founded before the Norman conquest of England, and Pius IX. can count more piedecessors than any potentate in the world. Even the overthrow of European States ensuing on the march of the French armies at the close of the list century oll'eis no tine analogy to the present revolutions The French armies had might ou their side, and, if Switzerland and Venice were convulsed at their approach, it was partly because the aid offered to revolutionists was knowu to he irresistible. But Garibaldi has had no such force at his command ; his troops were but a handful of men against the armies of the Neapolitan Monarch, and, except for the reinforcements he has received on his route, would be no match in numbers even for the mercenaries iu the service of the Pope. Nevertheless, we read day after day of such scenes and events as scarcely consist with any natural estimate of probabilities. Though Italy is certainly not in a state of decay, but is giving, on the contrary, unexpected signs of natioua! vigour, the political putrescence of its States transcends all examples on record. Administrations, armies and institutions are crum-

bling into fragments; Sovereigns are taking flight, and a simple adventurer has all the cities of the Peninsula at his call. The presence, or even the approach of Garibaldi, acts like a cityrnical solvent upon the organized politics of Southern Italy, and as soon as he appears the elements of the compound obey the attraction of new affinitives, and are crystallized under new forms. To what can we attribute so prodigious a result ? To the power of the man, or the previous condition of the people ? We must probably take both these causes into consideration if we wish really to understand the effect. There can be no doubt that for some years past the various Governments of Italy have existed only in outward show. They resembled those objects which in tropical countries are occasionally found so eaten out by ants that nothing but a thin crust of their substance remains They were undermined by secret societies, which buirowed beneath the surface of their institutions. They were deprived of all support from their subjects, and could not repose with confidence even ou their own soldiers. They relied for protection on Austria, and, when Austria was expelled from their confines, the system received its first great blow. Then came the liberation of Lombardy and the

T.. C R 0 (! X A ¥ I S, Duchies, followed by the strong contagion of I freedom ; while in Naples the Government, with suicidal folly, redoubled its efforts to repress the spirit of liberty. Still, for all this, it is uulikely that the catastrophe would have occurred, except for the marvellous power and equally marvellous successes of Garibaldi. The Neapolitans knew t heir own minds, but not their own strength or the weakness of their oppressors. To make this discovery it required the sagacity and daring of a genuine hero. Garibaldi has done in Naples what Clive did in Bengal, and after a similar fashion In each case the task proved perfectly easy ; but in each case, the adventure called either lor incredible discernment or superhuman courage The opposing force represented actually only' a phantom array, but it passed for a terrible reality until the predestined champion revealed its hollowness by a grasp. It is fortunate again for Italian freedom that it has been due so largely to tile powers ot a single man. Everybody can understand a hero. The name of Garibaldi comprehends and expresses all that the Italians at present either leel or desire. It reli ves them from the. contemplation of political theories, and shields 'hem from the designs of political agitators They know that iliey want liberty, and they know th.it Garibaldi brings it. They hear of him from day to day us always triumphant and always advancing. They learn that no obstacles either by sea or land have been any impediment to his career lb He landed in despite of the. hostile et, and be marched in Sicily

victoriously over the island in despite ot lie hostile garrisons. After this achievement the ciossed the. Straits, and repeated in Ca abria the exploits of his Sicilian campaign. At length he enters Naples þÿ a liberator, u coiiqucior, and a hero, and the Neapolitans are satisii d \\ hatever may come hereafter, they have now got Garibaldi, and with Garibaldi they arc content His p eseuce suggests no complications or jealousies. He represents simply Victory and Freedom. The Bourbons have 11 d belore his face, liberty follows in bis footsteps, and peace settles upon his track. No conditions more favourable to revolution could possibly be imagined The popular mind reposes with satisfaction and content upon the im igo of a hero, and all the troubles of a national n generation are quietly adjourned until the þÿhero w s ork be done. Thus far, then, wonderful as events have been, wo can find some explanation of them ; but it is only too evident that more must teinain behind. Garibaldi is Dictator, but Dictatorships are essentially the provisonal. reconstituted, and woik will be lruiight with Italy must be difficulties of all kinds. If the country passes whole and undivided under the sceptre ot King Victor Emmanuel, it will be such an expansion of the original project as he and his powerful ally never took into their consideration þÿ not to speak of the provincial animosities, which will not always be dormant. If new pretenders appear upon tbc stage, they will bring new com-

plications; it the old dynasties should be restored, it will be at the cost of peace. The truth is, the revolution is running away with its authois, and the element of which least account was taken has become the dominant element of the affair. The insurrection of Italians waste have played only a minor little might suffice for a part in the drama. It succour in Lombardy and a diveision in the Duchies, but uotliiug more. Lotnbaidy was to be made Italian instead of German, but that was all. Unfortunately for these speculations, the spiiil ot Liberty once unchained, pervaded, occupied, Fah- commanded the entire scene. Even the and peror Napoleon himself lost his power over events, and acknowledged his incapacity' to ratify his own conventions. The Italians, once relieved of the Austrians, took their own way, in spite of French or Piedmontese, and the scheme of allotments and compromises was superseded by a vision of united Italy. Garibalþÿdi own s fortunes have exactly expressed those of his country. A year ago he was a partisan leader in the service of the allies, conducting a handful of light troops along the skirts of the mountains, and feeling the way for the great army in his rear. He is now at the head of .a mighty movement, before which monarchies crumble, entering capitals from wliicli Kiogs have fled, and absorbing the aspirations of a eople in arms. Just so has it been with the talian Revolution. The liberation of Italy' commenced in the North on principles of compro-

mise and restriction, but it was presently prosecuted in the South on bolder terms, and it now compromises the whole country in its scope. That it may find its consummation in genuine freedom and permanent tranquillity is the universal wish of Englishmen.

Mr. þÿMcFarland sExcelsior Concept Troupe arrived here yesterday morning I delighting large audiences with some ex- from Sr. Thomas, where they have been cellent music. On arriving in the harbour the brass band of the Troupe struck up some tine airs ; and last evening they gave us an opportunity to judge of their attainments in vocal and instrumental music, which we take pleasure to pronounce as being ot no common order. This evening Mr. McFarland will give his first entertainment at the Danish School House; and, judging from the Programme for the evening, to which we refer our readers, our music-loving community will have an opportunity to indulge their taste at a moderate expense. In the absence of public amusement of any kind we hail with pleasure the arrival of this Troupe, and trust that the public will not be sparing of its patronage.

COMMUNICATH in To the Editor of the St. Croix Alia. Sir ! Listening to the voice of justice and reason, the Burgher Council lias at length effected a suitable reduction in the taxes to the Land Treasury, for which the community, more particularly the poorer class, can not but feel very thankful to the Honorable Board. As yet no reduction has taken place in the taxes to the State Treasury. There can however be no doubt that a suitable reduction in those taxes will also follow very soon, and most probably be witnessed at the time the present þÿyear s taxes become due, say May month next. It seems impossible that the Government, now, that the Burgher Council has set the example, should not yield; þÿ impossible that imposts should be upheld which, regulated a number of years ago, are equally disproportionate to the present value of real property and oppressive to the population, the enormity of which likewise is the more glaring after the similar imposts to the Landtreasury have been lowered and fixed at a reasonable rate. To express how confidently the community expects a corresponding boon on the part of the Government as has now been conferred on it by the Burgher Council, is the purport of these lines. Remaining Mr. Editor, Your obedient servant, X.

Mu. McFarland's musical entertainment last evening was well attended ; and the audience appeared to be amused. The music, both vocal and instrumental, was the chief attraction ; but, we regret to have observed, that the amusement experienced by those present diminished during the performance of the farces, which were badly selected and of too puerile a nature to be of much interest. We take this opportunity to suggest that a few more songs be substitued in the place of such pieces. Mr. McFarland intends to give an entertainment in Frederiksted on Saturday evening next, when we hope he will be as successful in drawing a full house as he was last evening.

The cries were mostly þÿ Viva Garibaldi þÿ! and þÿ L ltalia þÿuua. 1 did not hear þÿ Victor þÿEmmanuel much, but some men wore scarfs with his name. creatures, with ropy, rusty, long shaggy hair down their backs, just as you suppose wretches let out from years of imprisonment, gesticulating and looking frantic with joy. If they did represent prisoners, it is rather theatrical of them to keep their hair in such a mess all this time since they were let out. What was perfectly genuine was the beaming joy with which some clean young priests appealed to the balconies for sympathy. It is difficult to describe the excitement. After about an hour came up the red shirt on a carriage horse, with its blinkers on, to give warning that Garibaldi was coming, and then the cheeriug rose louder and louder ns tli e carriage came slowly along, and there he was without a bit of þÿState three red shirts with their backs to the carriage, himself and another man in the seat, of honour, and three more in a stuck-up rumble behind þÿ such fine old heads, with whitened beards, and all with their red shirts covered with purple stains, like English hunting coats which have been through sundry squire-traps. Their earnest, calm, sunburnt faces spoke of different work from running up and down a street shouting; but what could we poor little contemptible people do except shout and clap our hands All our party were assembled in the balcony, and, as happy chance would have it, long before he came up to us he turned his face our way, our group caught his eye, and until he came uuder our balcony, and had to turn his face quite up to see us, he kept his stea-
dy look fixed on us þÿ why, I þÿdon know, t for surely there were prettier dresses and fresher I'ace9 all around. 1 am too well content that chance had it so, so that we could watch delibe-

mine drop on the people below. 1 was told that I should never see so fine a sight as Paris wellcoming home her heroes last summer þÿ the Army of Italy, but this one carriage full of weatherbeaten elderly men was far grander þÿ not the sight of a Monarch who makes war for his own ambition in one way or other, but of the triumph of moral force and single-minded devotion The King had felt himself forced to fly, and 12 hours afterwards this simple hero entered all alone, like an envoy of Providence. Electro-Medical Apparatus, etc. þÿ M Despretz has recently submitted to the Paris Academy a new electro-medical apparatus, invented or combined by Ruhmkarff, and reduced to its simplest condition. A small box, in size about four cubic inches, contains an induction ; pile charcoal, in which nitric acid is replaced by Maiio- Davy's sulphate of mercury ; some handles, a brush, and some needles for distribution of the direct currents, or of the extra current to the surface of the patient. The manipulation of the apparatus is simple, no vapors are disengaged, and the apparatus will maintain its activity during a day. Thermo-electric currents are now extensively employed by Middledorp of Breslau, in surgory. With wires and blades of platina ot various dimensions, brought to a white electric heat, ho undertakes many operations commonly performed with cutting instruments. The heating agent is a þÿGrove battery, s and, properly performed in an operation, there is no hemorrhage of small vessels; the action is energetic and limited, can be sustained or cut off at pleasure, and applied through narrow passages, and to depths never attempted in ordinary cauterization. According to Middledorp, it admits of cutting, splitting, of cuttiog away, of cauterization on a single point or in rays, or over large surfaces, of stopping hemorrhage, of provoking inflamumtior <q certain tissues, of coagulation of the blood, of suppuration, aud the development of proper granulations.

Drinking at Meals. þÿ The opiniuu has often been advanced, that drinking during a meal is an obnoxious habit, but this is erroneous, lor the gastric juice may be diluted with a considerable quantity of water without losing its dissolving power iu the slightest degree. Only a super abundance of water would diminish or arrest the peculiar action of the matters contained in the digestive fluids. Large draughts of water, tlierelore, would be the most injurious with aliments rately the deep, true, sweet expression of those 1 difficult of digestion, like the fats, and hence the drinking of too much water after fat pork, for example, is to be avoided; but, in cases where fore that wonderful þÿ regard that I only let j soup does not constitute a regular part of the meal, drinking water is positively to be recommended.

Beer and wine at dinner are by some physicians considered hurtful only as taken in excess; in the latter case, the alcohol coagulates the albuminous substances not only of the food, but also of the digestive fluids, and thus disturbs dio-cstion. If taken in a moderate quantity, these liquids are believed to cause the meal to hold out longer; for the fact that a person is not so soon hungry again after a moal with wine as when water alone is taken with it, is to he accounted lor by the slower combustion of the constituents of tbo body, inasmuch as tbo alcohol imbibed takes possession of the inhaled oxygen. The general preference of warm food at dinnor is based on rational grounds; for a low temperature coagulates gelatine, and the fats coagulate, which are much more readily digested in a liquid state

(The Weekly Dispatch, London , September 30.) ITALY. We must not expect that a great kingdom can be built up with a wish. Still less can we have such a hope of a kingdom of Italy. Let us remember how it is to be constituted ; the elements to he used in the construction in many respects quite as hostile to the work as those actually repelling and resisting. Let us think of a population, from the highest to the lowest, purposely kept as ignorant and incited by motives as brutal as possible, lest they should revolt against the must sordid and profligate of tyrannies. Let us remember, too, what exterior ambitious and selfish intrigues have been at work ; what rights of property in human souls and bodies arc still asserted by die old vampire race ot monarchs, driven from tlnir prey, but repaying the curses of their saved victims with as deadly and almost as conscientious a bate. That any chance ot a kingdom of Italy should exist would be a miracle if we looked only at the outside of affairs aud made no account of that inner working spirit of generous manhood which lives in constant insurrection against tyranny and wrong. Wo all need such reflections at this moment, or this would not be the place to | make them. The uuity and safety of Italy are doubtless in great peril ; but yet that we should have to write and talk of the danger of such things, would have been an incredible wonder six months ago; their proximate existence was then only the dream of a few undaunted enthusi-

asts. It is tantalising beyond measure, no doubt, to get the perfect glimpse of a great probable good, and to see the cloud roll over the view, and threaten to efface it; but, alter all, tyranny in Italy is as yet far worse off than freedom. A little change in the apparent humour of one man would save the þÿpeople cause; s no such fortunate pivot exists on which that of the tyrants can revolve. Garibaldi in action is still himself. We have the details of his movement on the Volturno, and those who look at the map and see the position of Cajtizzo will not need to be told that in occupying that he has turned the left flank j lie has identified his feelings with ours, so lur as of his enemy, and that a battle must be fought by the þÿKing s forces to regain the ground, or the only line they can hope to hold is lost. A battle in the open field will not. suit his halfhearted troops. The news of disaster to the patriot forces are now fully accounted for by the imprudence of some of the regiments sent to make feints on the right of þÿBomba camp, s whose zeal for fighting made them eschew the purpose of the manoeuvre, and who paid on the spot for their disregard of orders. Then, turning to Victor þÿEmmanuel regular army, s we find its main body at Viterbo with an advanced guard at Mouterosi; and when we see that the French Commander in Rome omits all mention of any defence save that of Rome and Civita Vecchia from his programme, we find the actual occupation of the country almost settled between

the French and Royal Italian forces, whore outposts now approach each other as they could hardly be al owed to do unless by a perfect military understanding Moreover, the French garrison of Rome by no means permits such action to the remnant, of the Papal ragamuffins in the capital as may draw on the conflict across the slender neutral space ; and Latnoriciere, in no good odour with his countrymen for compromising the French military character, has already lost two of the forts of Ancona, aud awaits an assault on the main body the place. of It is impossible but that Francis II. must be utterly discouraged at the certainty that he has now foes, not friends, in his rear ; and Garibaldi, when he knows that the regular government of the King of Italy is in possession of almost all the Papal dominions, must pause before he ventures palpably to compromise the Italian unity by his own act in asserting any authority over I will the þÿKing f s orces which Victor Emmanuel dm s not grant him, or, worse yet, in lead.ng his brave but irregular bands to au attack barred by the Royal army of Italy. If we may accept the surety of the þÿ Constiþÿtutionel, France has no intent whatever of cause. making war on Victor Emmanuel in the þÿPope s The To protect the þÿPontiff person s and the seat of his episcopate is all that. Napoleon pre tends. The words of his semi-official journal þÿ are emphatic, and every way worthy of note : þÿ France has increased her body of troops at Rome ; she will combat revolution if it dares
approach that city ; it is her right as a Catholic Power ; by extending her interference beyond that, she would become an object of suspicion to

s r.4J ® Ci Si l & Vl I) $ « Europe, and hateful to þÿItaly. It is quite well to be assured that Napoleon sees exactly how lie is estimated by the Italians, aud on what his remaining popularity will theu depend. Indeed, in the meditation of the great struggle, the conjecture has more than once crossed our thoughts, that þÿGaribaldi savowal of bitter hatred against the authors of the annexations is, possibly, less a denunciation of vengeance lor the seemingly irrevocable past, than a fierce warning for the future. If he holds back Sicily aud Naples, it may be that he does so lest they should be bartered against Sardinia and Genoa. Even the þÿ opinion, þÿTimes, the has tendered him cause pseudo-representative of English enough tor this most galling suspicion. He may forgive the surrender of Ids native Nice ; he would die rather than see the treason repeated. We would hope that he may indeed be far above the influences that seem to act upon him. be so well kept out of mischief nowhere else r May it not be that he amuses some of them with office and courtesy, lest they should embarrass him, as he, for tire moment, appears to be cm barrassing Victor Emmanuel ? W e are but guessing, but we certainly do not wish prematurely to undervalue the hero whose genius has hitherto been the vivifying power of the Italian resurrection In the authenticity of the letter asserted to have been written to him by Kossuth, urging him to rally tirmiy to the King, we are inclined to put faith Kossuth h is learned the lesson of true liberal policy in this country,

to educate bis sous in our schools. He is imbued with our wariness and our firmness, and it he counselled Garibaldi at all, would be very likely to do so in a British spirit. Her Tory statesmen, of the deepest dye, would have nothing to do with we a Holy Al- liance thirty-tour yeais ago, before, may say ; this couutry had learned to read and write ; before its people had entered upon the direct dealing with their own affairs. It Russia weie again to occupy Hungary, or to garrison the Austrian coast of the Adriatic against the Italians, exactly in proportion to her activity would she force on the action of England in defence of the Italian cause, aud strengthen our good understanding with France. Herein is the more than triumph, the world-wide blessing ot our recent policy, that wo stand strong and

unshackled, ready at a moment to throw our moral weight into the scale of justice whenever it may be too heavily counterpoised, and that our moral weight is backed by a physical power and a national resolution which no opponent care rashly to put to the test. COMMUNICATION. To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis. Dear Sir, I take the liberty of asking your opinion on the following subject : A few days ago the þÿKing s urveyor Mr. Scheli.eriip was requested by me to survey the property No. 8, East Street, branding at same time two bound-posts, for which lie charged 6$. This survey was considered expedient in eonsequence of my intention to build a cistern on the place, lie then demurred to my extending the cistern to the fence (facing the West) asserting that the fence was four feet on the public ground. This fence stands about five feet higher than the street on a solid mass of rocks, and, circa eight feet from the gutter on the same side of (lie street. By reference to the records, I find the former owner came in possession of the above named properly in the year 1837 aud this fence has beou there a number of years, if not contemporary with the purchase. Although having these considerations fas I thought) in my favour, I nevertheless desired the surveyor to petition the Royal Government soliciting a grant for the building of the cistern to be exteuded to the fence, which lie peremptorily refused doing aud, at same lime intimated to me, that independent of the 6$ already paid, the work could not proceed unless another amouut of 2$ was paid him for a certificate ; even allowing that 1 commenced building four feet from the fence.

So tiiat you should be in a position to form a just opinion of what has been said respecting the locality and its bearing I would particularly beg that you call and see the place, judging impartially whether building up to the fence (the same being nearly two feet within the extremity of the gallery and the gallery on a line with a house just aside of it and having no gallery) can be considered by the surveyor iu any' reasonable way, as an encroachment on the public ground. Trusting that a knowledge of the laws by | which he is guided iu this respect is familiar to you (such as keeping the proper lino towards the street when building &c. &o.) I will feci thankful for your opinion. 1 can however only come to this conclusion that private motives must actuate the surveyor in his petty annoyances towards me in this affair, especially when his refusal to petition the Royal Government on this matter, is taken into consideration. Respectfully, JAS. P. BRULEY St. Croix, Christiansted25th September I860.

From the London Times , August 31. An epidemic is at this moment spreading itself over Europe, and England is at least as subject to it as any of her neighbours. If sedative and tranquillizing remedies would have availed to calm this disorder of the nerves, we should long since have been restored to perfect health. We have had administered to us every species of soothing prescription, but all iu vain ; the disorder does not yield to the treatment, and every fresh practitioner retires baffled by its obstinacy and inveteracy. The name of this disorder is Distrust. Confidence, we are told on high oratorical authority, is a plaut of slow growth ; but Distrust, though it springs up much more speedily, is much more difficult to eradicate. It is no fault of ours ; we desire nothing better than t» return to our old state of absolute security, to the glorious days preceding the Crimean War, when we had not 20 guns fit for service in the realm, when we had no Channel Fleet, when our army at home was scarcely worth speakiug of, and when, confident iu our own eai nest de ire to be at peace with all the world, we considered oui selves perfectly safe Behind the rampart of our own good intentions. Those days are gone, and we have instead 30,000,000/. of naval and military expenditure, a loan of 9,000,000/. for fortifying our dockyard, be-idiswe know not what impests levied on our gallant youth in the form of the services of a hundred and fifty' thousand Volunteers If any amount of fair speaking or fair writing could convince us that these

tilings were unnecessary, we should long ago have laid aside this attitude of most unwelcome preparation, and betaken ourselves þÿ to our more congenial instruments the plough- once moro sliaio and the shuttle. We have been proof to the þÿEmperor s letter, sli.ll we now yield to the blandishments of his Ambassador / M. de Persigny has imny claims to our attention ; he has resided long in England, he is one of the, stanchest friends this country lias in France, aud his openness and honesty tire beyond all question. Let us see, then, what he can uige calculated to dispel our uneasiness, and locmivince us that this practical, phlegmatic nation, is at. this moment deceived by phantoms of its own imagination. M. de Persigny, as President, of the General Council for tire Department of the Loire, proposes to himself to examine the momentous question as to the probability of the maintenance of peace in Europe. We only wish that the statements he makes were as incontestable as that his intentions are friendly. This, however, unfortunately, is nut the case, lie tells us that the þÿEmperor programme s at Bordeaux has not been changed ; that programme we, in common, we believe, with all Europe, understood to be Peace; but it appears that we weio mistaken, and that when the Emperor spoke of Pe ace he only meant to repudiate þÿ þÿ the inlieritance of mere fighting for the sake of avenþÿ the defeats of the first ging þÿEmpire. War for any other purpose is not disclaimed, and we

must, therefore, for the future read the celebrated declaration of Bordeaux in this very restricted sense, which leaves perfectly open to the Empire wars þÿ for the sake of þÿideas, wais for the sake of natural boundaries, wars waged for any purpose whatever, except vengeance for the reverses of the First Napoleon. Two questions, we are told, were pending before the inauguration of the Empire þÿ one of the East, the other of Italy', neither of which admitted of a pacific solution, hut both were settled with great promptitude; and, as the next best tiling to no war at all is a short war, we presume that the Peace of Villafranca must be considered as another verification of the declaration of Bordeaux. Nor can wo feel quite convinced that France þÿ lias iccognized the þÿ principle of non-iuterveution in þÿItaly so long as she occupies Home iu force, and thus imposes on the subjects of the Pope a domination which would not last twenty-four hours after those forces were withdrawn. M de Persigny next proceods to tell us that the apprehensions respecting the Rhine frontier and t lie invasion of England are utterly without foundation. The Rhine is no longer a þÿ strate þÿ þÿfrontier, and France is no much gic stronger when Germany is divided that she would nevot purchase the frontier of the Rhine by conceding German unity. A very celebrated writer of the last century asserted as a cardinal point in a stupendous system of teaching, that the year 17o7 marked an important crisis in the spiritual history of our race. He predicted (mystically as some may suppose) that after tho petiod here specified, the influxes of that subtle and vital magnetism which constitutes the intellectual and moral aliment of mankind, would he so far changed, or rather discriminated, as to admit of more treedom and clearness of thought ; that higher states of general intelligence would consequently supervene, and that the result would be the gradual outworking of most important changes iu all the political and ecclesiastical affairs the Without stopping to inquire into ot mankind. alleged facts or theoretical grounds on which these assertions were based, we can but acknowledge, on reviewing the history of the past hundred years, that developments such as wore predicted as resulting from these alleged changes in the channels of human inspiration, havo conspicuously appeared, from whatever cause, and that the same are still iu that active progress which gives promise ol a no distant future realization of all that was foretold in respect to political and ecclesiastical reconstructions. It is a conspicuous tact that the latter part of the eighteenth century witnessed the initiament of an intellectual, revolutionary, and general meliorative activity such as was scarcely known to previous history, uud this activity has been

continued, with acceleration, down to the present moment. One hundred years ago the masses both ol Europe and ot the then in. ant state of America were in a statu of supine acquiescence in tho oppressions ol their tyrants, whilo thick darkness covered the earth as witli a mantle. But not long subsequen t to that

period, the mentality of tho world began to he inspired with unwonted vigor, and commenced a career of brilliant scientific and artistic discoveries, while the masses at the same time grew restive under the burdens of political and social wrongs, and clamorous for reform. Nor was this simply a new phase in the development of movements and aspirations which had previously been in active operation, but the start was sudden aud seemingly from a newly created impulse. This will best appear iu the light of a few specifications. Before Franklin, for example, there was comparatively nothing known of the now tremendous and important science of electricity ; before Davy, Priestly, aud Lavoisier, little was known of chemistry ; notwithstanding the previous important discoveries of Coperuieus, Galileo, Kepler, Newton, and La Place, it may be said that comparatively little was known oven of astronomy until the Horschels directed tlioir tremendous tubes to tho Milky Way, sounded it to its depths, construeted a diagram of its shape and proporand discovered universes ot universes silently rolling in the iufinito depths of the spaces beyond. Nor was anything known of the absorbing and important science of geology before the first crude forms of its doctrines were inaugurated by Werner and Hutton; nothing was kuown of phrenology before Gall and Spurzheitn, nothing of animal magnetism before almost nothing of labor-saving ntachiuery before the iuveutions of Hargreaves, Arkwright and Crompton, nothing, practically, ot

steam locomotion before Fulton, nothing ot sunpainting before Daguerre and nothing of electric telegraphing beloro Morse. All these, with thousands of collateral, subordinate, yet more or less important discoveries and inventions, have been made during the last hundred years, withe during the same period a free, populous, and enlightened nation has sprung up on this Western continent, flourishing in all those arts, sciences, and internal improvements that arc characteristic of a high degree of civilization þÿ and which, extending its dominion from the Atlantic to the Pacific shores, connect with the old world and completes a zone of civilization spanning the whole globe ! Aud while this consummation has hern verging to its lulfilmeut, the buried cities and monuments of the Orient have been in process of exhumation, and the long-forgotten wisdom bodied in their inscriptions and mystic symbolisms have been measurably thrown open to the light, by the indefatigable labors of a Layard, a Rawlinson, and the French savans; and as an interesting climax to this strange and general progression, old Asia lias just sent forth a deputation of her most inquisitive children to sock knowledge in the region of the rising sun, and tho hoary empires of the East are sitting at tho feet of Young America Thus has the last become first, and the first last \

It may therefore be assorted that the last hundred years has been signalized by more substantial progress to the race than the thousand years which preceded The march is still on- þÿ ward with accelerated speed. What shall bo the þÿ conclusion of the whole þÿmatter? Wo know not its particulars ; its generals aro a subjeot of mathematics. The prophetic stone has been cut out of the mountain without hands ; it has smitten the age of superstition, of tyranny, of places, oppression, has and broken and of wickedness in high and low it, and the stone is now in process of becoming a mountain itself that will fill the whole earth. The mountain is the spiritual Mount. Zion whose watchmen will see eye tc eye, and from whoso sublime summits will be proclaimed tbe law of universal brother hood under the reign of one King who is the Father of all.

LIGHTNING. The remark is often made that casualties by lightning are annually increasing in number, notwithstanding the multiplied precautions taken to guard against them. But. it may well be doubted whether they occur more frequently, in proportion to the increased population, than in former years. There are now so many newspapers in the rural districts, that every local incident of the kind is quickly caught up, put into print, and sent off on its travels. It must be to the modern thoroughness with which they are reported by the local press that the idea nt their increased frequency is to he attributed ; for a careful record kept by Mr. Meriam of Brooklyn shows that there is but little annual variation in the number of these casualties In 185S there were 56 persons killed aud 66 injured by lightning, while in 1859 there weie 76 killed and 44 injured, being two less than the year before. During the many years of observation which this gentleman has devoted to the phenomena of lightning, he says that no case of death lias happened to a peison lying on an iron bedstead, or in a liou-e or building having a hi. tallic r. of. Heavers that persons in iron buildings, iron vess Is, within railroad cars, on hoard steamboats or ocean steamers, or in vessels furnished with metallic conductors, continue to enjoy complete protection from death or injury from lightning. 8o also with those, in ordinary buildings furnished with pioper conductors. Mr. Meriam thinks that thunders and lightnings are engaged in other labors

than those usually recorded as lightning incidents. Distant thunder, for instance, will curdle milk and stop the fermentation of þÿbrewer s yeast, while active lightning putrefies the fresh meat hanging on the þÿbutcher sstall The potato rot will þÿj be rt identified as i lie result of electrical iiiiluenci s. Diseases in the human system have long been susp. ctcd of a similar oiigin, while others are undoubtedly aggravated by this mysterious agent of the Almighty. þÿ< holer i, and kindred complaints, are largely influenced by thunder and lightning, and so with yellow fever ; lorAn countries where no thunder and lightning are active, these, scourges are unknown. India, when1 the lightning is awlul and the thunder terrific, has in cholera an ever present scourge, while California, where the thunder gusts is unknown, has b, eu pronounced the healthiest climate ill (lie world. It is renntikable that large cities enjoy an almost perfect immunity f, om danger to life bv lightning. This remark applies as we.l to American as to European cities. Between 1800 aud 1851, not a single death by lightning is recorded as having occurred in Paris, while throughout France, from 1835 to 1852 the average annual number of deaths from the same cause was 72. In 1835 die number killed was 111. During 30 years, in w hieh 750,000 deaths occurred in London, two only had been prnduced by lightning Twenty-five per cent of all the deattis from this cause happen to persons under trees From this data it is evident that

liglitniug finds mom victims in the open country than iu cities. There are definite reasons for this immunity enjoyed Iry citizens. Largo towns are made up of lolty buildings, multitudes of which are covered with metallic roofs, from which tin or iron gutters lead off the rain water. They contain many churches, most of which I have ostentatious spires armed with lightning rods. Private dwellings ate protected in the same tvay, so that the city iu reality bristles with metallic points, each of which, presented to the thunder cloud, discharges silently but surely, a portion of its destructive þÿenergy . This vast array of conductors grouped up within a limited area, must, of necessity, carry off' the electricity of an overhanging cloud, not, it is true, as rapidly as it, is generated iu þÿNature s great laboratory, but rapidly enough to mitigate its intensity. When the bolt does fall, it lights on some one of these multitudinous points, which thus performs its wonderful office of carrying the explosion harmlessly off. Although Franklin identified the flash from a thunder-cloud as electricity, yet it was reserved to Andrew Crosse to dissect the cloud itself i By u most elaborate arrangement of metallic

wires, he succeeded in obtaining an insight into tiie tremendous composition of a thunder-cloud, such as the cheap and temporary apparatus of Franklin was incompetent to afford, and such, indeed, as his mind never contemplated. > Franklin resolved the grand problem, while Orosse added the details. He stretched a vast net-work of wins acro-s the tops of the trees as to prevent a dispersion of the fluid. composing a large forest, and so iusulated These them wires were feelers thiust out to gather in from distant clouds and fi >gs a more terrific volume ot electricity than human temerity had ever ven- at tured to collect, so that it might bo examined his leisure in the laboratory. This was a chamber with an arched roof, filled with voltaic batteries, electric jars, galvanic piles, and other paraphernalia of the electrician. Subtle streams i of the mysterious fluid flowed in in silent but ceaseless currents, piling up little mineral fabrics, and fashioning the obedient atoms into exquisite crystraliizaiious. Here, too, its fiercest wrath might any at moment -be developed lor this network of wires poured its peril >us aecretious into a large brass conductor fixed and insulated on a table When these accretions became dangerously great, a contrivance permitted him to turn oft' the current, and discharge it into the earth without entering the chamber. An arrangement of halls enabled him in to the smallest quantity ot electricity detect the atmosphere 't hese halls gave token ot an approach-

ing thundercloud, long, before it made itself j known to the mul titude. Spark following spirk and explosion succeeding txplosiou, rapidly, icpeaied, and increasing iu energy as the commotion gathered force, enabled the adventurous observer to look into and dissect the cloud, and to listen to its language, iu his chamber, long before those outside could distinguish even its i muttering-. As the margin of the approaching cloud overhung the net-work of wiret in the tree-tops, a spitk was seen, a detonation heard, and these flashes and explosions were repeated at interva s. A pause ensued, and then the app iratns gave forth another set of sparks and strappings, hut differing from the first, which wire negative, while these were positive After a second poise a more energetic display succeeded, but of negative electricity, to he succeed, d by another display of positive. Then followed a more numerous and brilliant succession of fl ,shes, announcing that another z oic ol vapor was sweeping by, to he followed, af,er a luiel interval, by a correspond, ng zoue ol positive electricity. As the cloud drew nearer the intervals of repose became shorter, and a stream of living fi'C was seen to pour from one conductor to tire other When the centre of the cloud stood directly over the tree tops the effect was awful. The wites, plunging iuto the electric atmosphere which invariably precedes and surrounds n thunder cloud, suckul out the lightning I rein its vet y heart, and it leaped madly from

ball to ball, iiistuut d- atli being iu every explosion to him who iinpi udcutly approached too near. This terrific exhibition of the forces embodied in the cloud continued for a longer or shorter period, according to the magnitude ot the storm aud the cons, queut disturbance of the electrical equilibrium. As the excited vapors rolled by, the explo-ions diminished iu number, arid a scries of twin eruptions alternating with periods of repose, showed that the latter half ol the cloud corresponded in its eloctriml anal guneuts with the lormer halt. Gradually the languid flish and snap announced that the disturbance had ceased, and that the storm was traveling over sonic uew locality, there to let loose the um xpend, d reiuuaut of its wrath This dangerous but really successful effort to explore tlie mysteries which arc locked up in the thunder-cloud, has yielded no practical result. The science of protecting human life from lightning remains precisely where Franklin left it. Ilis single discovery placed it, at a single bound, in the front rank of the definite arts, and we know no more now thau he taught us a century ago. His first lightning rod lie put up on his own liou.-e in Market street, Philadelphia. This rod descended to the second story window, where it entered the chamber of the philosopher. Here, being disconnected the distance of a few feet, the intervening space was occupied by a string of hells At the approach of a thundercloud the same disturbances were noticed aud
recorded which Mr. Ciosso bus so elaborately caused to bo repeated The bells were rung by the electricity as it passed in a silent, stream through the rod to the earth.

s T- o U O' I X V I s . This presence of an electrical atmosphere has sometimes exhibited the most remarkable plienomena. The great lightning storm of .Tunc, 1848, was especially productive of them. Mr. þÿCooper extensive s rolling-mill at 1 teuton, N. J., seemed to be charged in every part with electricity. Though that storm extended over a j surface of 700 miles, yet no place witnessed a J more singular display of its mighty energies than Trenton. The lightning struck the earth there j repeatedly. A workman at the rolling-mill at- j tempted to lower the iron damper, which was connected with iron chains, but lie no sooner laid bis hand on the latter than he received a shock which prostrated him. A second workman repeated the attempt, and was in turn kuocked down, while the third also received a severe shock. A fireman attempted to stir the melted iron in the furnace, hut the instant his iron stirrer touched the fluid metal he received a violent shock. Other similar facts occurred, showing that the whole atmosphere avas charged with electricity to an extraordinary extent, and that chains, bars, furnaces, and even the melted metal, were silently acting as conductors between the cloud and the earth, giving out neither shock nor spark unle-s touched by the unconscious workman. The masses of metal which surrounded the 300 hands employed in the mill were so many potent protectors ; hut the same precautions should he used to guard against the electrical atmosphere which invariably precedes and surrounds a thunder cloud, as

against the cloud itself. A wire one-quarter inch thick will effectually protect any building, providing there be a point of stiff metal set up ou every prominent part, with as uiauy outlets into the ground as there are points in the air, the whole being connected by cross wires extending over the building. Galvanized wire is preferable to all others, as it is not liable to oxidation. The greater t lie quantity of iron, and the more numerous the outlets, the greater the safety. This is iu accordance with þÿFranklin sdirections, except that the quantity of iron is increased. A large building should have some hundreds of feet of rod, and any building whatever should have not less than two points aud two outlets. There is a good reason lor this apparent profusion of iron. Explosions of electricity vary in intensity, some being very feeble, while others are of awful power. No certaiu calculation can he made as to whether the coming shock will he light or heavy heuce it is prudent to guard agaiust the latter, as in doiug so we effectually disarm the former. A light shock will he carried off hy a single rod without injury ; hut the discharging power of such a rod tiling uniform with its receiving power, because of its single outlet, an explosiou on its poiut may occur, clanged with so prodigious a volume ol electricity that the capacity the rod is not great of enough to carry it off. Herein lies the great danger of nu insufficient conductor. The discharging power being fixed and limited, any

excess of electricity will leave the conductor, fly off iuto the house in search of another, whether it he the stove-pipe or the human body, aud do its deadly work. Innumerable cases where such results have followed an excessive discharge on a conductor having a single outlet to the earth are ou record Accounts are often published of injury to buildings, though protected hy conductors; hut careful examination into the facts ol the case has iuvariably shown that though the conductor was free from defect, its capacity was too small to break up aud carry off a heavy shock. It follows, then, that the discharging power of a conductor must be equal to its receiving power ; that a building should be armed with poiuts on all its prominent projections, because no calculation cau be made on which prominence the shock may fall, that these receiving poiuts should have numerous discharging puiuts descending to moisture iu the earth, aud that the whole should be connected by wires in several directions across the roof, so that whichever point may happen to receive the shock will he aided by tile entire network of metal in instantly mitigating its inten.-ity by distributing it over a large surface, and passing it þÿoft by numerous outlets. TllO fluid concentrated in this shock hud been previously distributed over the surface of an immense body of clouds. How uuretisonahle it is to expect a single discharging point to pass þÿoft the volume of electricity accumulated in so great a body of
vapor. It is for these reasons that the cheap conductors are found so often mere traps, bring-
ing the dangerous element into a building, in- . stead of leading it away.

The tranquillity of the city lias not, been disturbed, and tbe same enthusiasm still prevails The Elmo and the other forts have surrendered, i he English Admiral has paid a visit, to Gari baldi, who afterwards went, on hoard the Hannibal, the English Ambassador being picsent. It is said that the King on leaving Naples ordered the bombardment ol the town and the burning of the Royal Cuslle. It is even asserted that the original of that order has been found. A report is also current that the King will quit Gaeta with his army of 30,000 men, and will join General Lamoriciere. The King has formed a n w Royalist Ministry, the members of which are Caselli, Canofuri, ITlIos, and Gcrolamo. The Austrian, Russian, Prussian, and Spanish Ministers, and the Papal Nuncio, have followed the King to Gaeta. The whole army of Garibaldi will arrive at Naples in four days, and, with the insurgent bands, the total force will be raised to 80,000 men The revolution is everywhere triumphant. It. is said that the Dictator is about to march to Umbria. The Bixio and Medici brigade s have just arrived in the port. Baron Brenier has not protested against the disembarkation of the Sardinian troops. A proclamation of Garibaldi to the Neapolitans, issued yesterday, has been published. Garibaldi, in this proclamation, says that the annexation will be effect, d when he shall be able to proclaim it from the top ot the Quirinal. DEPARTURE OF THE EX-KING FOR SPAIN. The Potrie announces that the King ot Naples left Gaeta on the 12th inst., ou board a Spanish frigate, for Sevilla.

THE FRENCH ISLANDS. All attention is concentrated upon the question of Colonial Free Trade, from which g eat commercial advantages are anticipated. The basis of this proposed freedom of commerce are stated as follows: þÿ þÿ Importations, under the national Hag, of such portions of the colonial productions ns will continue to be sent to the home markets; and importations by nil flags of such portions as it may be found desirable to Send into foreign þÿmarkets. This proposal is justified by the reasoning, þÿ That colonial sugar, called for in the course of commercial affairs, will always c me, the conditions being equal, to seek preference in the market of its parent state ; but, should that market be found glutted, a d this sugar cannot, he disposed of there except at a Ess. then let it have the liberty of being offered elsewhere ; there is no reason, not even political, to transcend the economical reason which requires that a production should not be forced to be sold at a hos in Havre or Marseilles, when it might obtain a remunerating price in London or New þÿYoik. The following interesting letter from Port-au-Prince appeared in a recent number of tlie Nar York Herald: þÿ In my last I alluded to the efforts made by our President to luster agriculture aud induce the country people to pay more attention to the matter. As I have already advised, each parish will have an agricultural school aud fifty pupils, chosen by the Government, and educated at each Iree of exp use. The plan is au excellent one and meets with universal approbation. These model iarms, placed in the well-settled districts of each parish, of course will atiract attention, and to each the surrounding planters can go for information, and perhaps in a lew years these farms will distribute seeds at a very trifling expense. The President orders all the officers of the country districts to give the labourers every facility ; it would he well, too, to require from six to seven þÿhours labour, or exemption only by fine, from every inhabitant, and if labour is chosen it should he enforced, as it was under the rule of that stern old Governor, Cbristophe. In several of the districts where water is required it is proposed, to form Artesian wells, and at Gonaivcs, it is said, one is already ordered. At Jcrcmiu water will litlier he led into the city, or such a well will be dug. The drinking water now used by this eity, one of the most flourishing of the country, is brought nearly a league by donkeys. Geffrard vows it is an outrageous waste of labour, and shall last no loDger. An engineer is ordered to examine the spot and

report the best mode of introducing water. Since writing last the number of Louisiana emigrants at the districts of St. Marc lias been iueieuscd. These people having sent persons before them to ascertain what advantages might be obtained by emigration to Hay ti, were satisfied with the report, and having readily obtained a grant of exceedingly rich land from the government, have since been coining over in parties of forty or fifty persons. They say that there are many more on their way, and that the s. vero laws enacted in some of tlie Missis sippi Slates against negroes will induce a large number to follow them. The economical modes of cultivating their fields, and the tools they bring with them have caused tho outside negroes to open their eyes, and will probably lead to many improvements in tlie neighbourhood. You will he surprised to learn that among tho emigrants there is a good deal of money, some of them having largo sums of money, which they bring with them. For poorer emigrants who bring but their labour, the Government offers to pay towards the passago money $15 lor those in the middle life, and 8 for children or old men. If the blacks of your city wish to get on in tho world lot them send a deputation and look into their prospects here, and it t Ley find them satisfactory they can get rich lands for tho asking, and can make engagements to have part of their passage paid to their new homes

From the London Times , September 14. We have not hud long to wait fur the decision of tiic King of Sardinia upon the advice proffered to him by the French semi-official press. The troops of Victor Emmanuel have entered the Roman territories, and war lias liegun in good earnest. General Cialdiui has taken Pesaro, which was already announced as being in a state of insurrection, and with the town twelve, hundred Germans and Monsignor Bella have fallen into his hands. Orvieto has also surrendered. This is a dashing beginning of the campaign, and a step that cannot be tenanted Sardinia has abandoned the temporizing policy which she had adopted since the armistice ol Villafranca She no longer oscillates backwards aud fotwatd-, but throws in her lot with the Italian revolution. Policy has done her work, all that negotiation, all that balancing and temporizing coul I effect lias been iffected, and there is nothing 1 It for it but to fight it out manfully to the last. We may easily imagine the motives that have driven Sardinia to this decisive step. So long as she aud her King wete the only recognized representatives of the Italian movemeut she might feel herself at liberty to consult her own safety, and await quietly the march of events ; but the Italiau movement is no longer under the exclusive direction of the Sardinian Government. Victor Emmanuel has in Garibaldi a must formidable competitor þÿ a man of that mould of which the successful lcadets of great popular uprisings are made, þÿ a man utterly regardless

ot self, and not to he acted on by any of the meaner motives by which common nu n are to he controlled The conqueror of Naples and Sicily is quite certain not to arrest his advance at the frontier of the Roman States. The momentum that he has gained seems sufficient to earry him over all the resistance which the States of the Church can offer, and to bring him with a violent shock iuto collision with the Austrian power in Venice. For such a consummation the Sardiuian Government is not prepared. It sees plainly that if things hold their present course a little longer it will be in the power of Garibaldi to drag Piedmont as well as all the rest of Italy into a conflict with Austria, and to force her to risk all she has gained in an encounter where the probabilities of success are against her. She must, therefore, at whatever cost or risk, make herself once more mistress of the revolution. She must lead, that she may not be forced to follow. She must revolutionize the Papal States, in order that she may put herself in a position to arrest a dangerous revolutionary movement against Venetia. There is some reason to think that in a recent interview the Emperor of the French has been induced to see tilings from this point of view, and that uo danger is appreheuded on the side of France. These motives are amply sufficient to account for the decisive movement of Victor Emmanuel. He lives iu revolutionary times, when self-preservation lias superseded all other considerations, and it would be

childish to apply to his situation the maxims of international law which are applicable to periods of trauquility . These being the motives which have impelled Piedmont to draw t lie sword, we have next to see what are the grounds on which she justifies the step. These grounds are two þÿ the extract dinary misrule and oppression of the Papal Government, and the presence of large bauds of foreign mercenaries, by which t lie couutry is oppressed and terrorized. The object is said to be to give the people au oppoituuity of expressing their own wishes and the re-establisbinent of civil order. The King promises to respect the seat of the Chief of the Church þÿ Romo, we, suppose, and its immediate environs; but, whilo holding out this assurance, tile manifesto speaks of the Pope and his advisers in terms of bitterness and acrin unusual iu the present age, even in a declaration of war. lie will teach the people forgiveness of offences, and Christian tolerance to the Pope and his Generals. Ho denounces the misguided advisers of the Pontiff and the fanaticism of the wicked sect, which conspires against his authority and the liberties of the nation. This is harsh language, and is not inconsistently seconded by the advanoe into the States of the Church of an army of 50,000 men. We have not scrupled to avow the opiniou that the motives which urge the King of Sardi-

s T. CHOI X AVIS , nia to invade the territory of a neighbour with whom lie is nominally at peace, and whom lie has already stripped of half his dominions, are not wholly, or even principally, those which his declaration puts forward ; and yet we do not scruple to say that we heartily wish the King success. For this we have many reasons. In the present condition of Southern and Northern Italy it is quite impossible to prevent a people outraged and trampled upon like the subjects of the Pope front rising in premature, and, if their own strength alone be considered, in hopeless, insurrection. At Fossombrone the insurrection has been put down by force, and the telegraph informs us of what we can well believe, þÿ that scenes similar to those ef Perugia have been enacted. The war began between the Pope and His subjects before the Piedmontese crossed the frontier, and we well know how the soldiers of the Cross made war. We do not wish to see Lumoricicre and his Condottieri carrying fire, slaughter, and violation thiough the dominions ot the Pope, and justifying the rule of the Vicegerent of Heaven by deeds which Hell itself might blush to look upon. This hand of mercenaries is a menace and an insult to the rest of Italy. It has been called into existence lor no other purpose than to oppress the subjects of the Pope, and to put down by armed force the rising revolution; and we do uot see that the Powers against which this army has been levied are hound to wait till a suitable opportunity presents itself

for the Free Companions, satiated with slaughter and rapine in the States of the Cliuich, to exercise their trade at the expense of Tuscany or the Legations. Then theie is the intolerable oppression of the þÿPope Government s The best pi oof of that oppression is the fact that the Pope dares not trust his own subjects with arms, but places himself, like Dionysius of Syracuse, in tiie bauds of foreign mercenaries. The spectacle of a people kept down by such means is an outrage on the civilization of the age, and a danger and menace for all the rest ot Italy'. Till some Government be established in the centre of Italy which can he maintained without ten thousand French troops to garrison the capital, and five and twenty thousand foreign mercenaries to sack insurgent towns, it is in vain to hope for peace. We freely' admit that nothing hut the extremity of the evil could justify tile step which Sardinia lias taken, hut we think that step is justified. The evil would not cure itself. The locusts would not depart while a blade of grass remained for them to devour, and the mercenaries would remain while wealth, beauty, and revenge for the hatred in which they are held by the people had still temptations to offer. For all these teasons we think the King of Sardinia is entitled to the sympathy of Englishmen in the war in which lie lias engaged. We wish him cordially success, and that his success may he rapid as well us decisive. s- FRANCE.

The following letter from St. Petersburg, tinted the 4th inst., is evidently intended to prove that the Russian public is not favourable ti> Austria or to its Government : þÿ þÿ Public opinion, excited by the news from Italy and Germany, has been too much diverted, I iu my opinion, from domestic matters. At this moment people are discussing, with more than ordinary animation, the leaning which our Government shows towards Austria. I apprized you already of this fact, and 1 had good reasons for doing so. I cannot describe to you the painful sensation created throughout the population by this change of policy. In private society in the couutry, even in the þÿpeasant s cabin and iu the barracks, angry words and curses against Austria are heard. Both officers and soldiers ask whether Russian blood is again to be shed for Austria, who is hated for her had government by the people under her sway, whom she has so often deceived? They further inquire whether Russia lias not sufficiently experienced Austrian ingratitude without making another trial? The feeling ot aversion for that Power is universal, and Imust add that anything Get man is not, to the taste of the lower classes. You are aware that there is no country less known than ours. Foreigners, particularly Frenchmen, entertain an idea that there is no

public opinion in Russia. The error arises from our not having institutions like Western nations þÿ a Legislative Assembly for example. Well, they are much mistaken There is a well-pronounced public opinion in Russia. It is not always visible at the surface, but it has deep root in the country, and shows itself on great occasions. It is then capable of every effort and of every sacrifice. But if it he opposed, then it offers a passive resistance, and produces such obstacles as will paralyze any political policy of which it disapproves. If our army were again to be placed at the disposal of Austria you would see the consequences of our national antipathy. The reception given to the Emperor by the nobility of Moscow was most enthusiastic. The reconciliation between them i- complete, hut everybody asks ,v hat the emancipation of the peasants will gain by it. This great measure seems to sleep, and Count Panine, the President of the Commission, when questioned on the subject makes no reply. The summer here has Leeu tenihle, aud has been marked by epidemic diseases, which have caused terrific ravages. The cemetery at St. Petersburg lias not for many years received so many corpses within so short a space of time. It was found convenient to attribute the mortality to cholera, hut on this occasion, I can assure you, the cholera was calumniated, and the cat closeness and the apathy of the authorities are more iu fault. You ate aware that St. Petersburg is traversed by various canals. Now these canals

which re nder great service in the conveyance of provisions, have never been cleaned out since they were made, and they have become the receptacles of every kind of filth. In winter they are frozen, hut in summer < m i t a poisonous effluvia. The intense heat of this summer has considerably increa-ed the þÿdanger.

The Assembly, in their reply, assured his Excellency ot their anxiety to concur with him in all measures that had for their object the prosperity and welfare of the Colony. to submit measures for their consideration, in the shape of bills. Neither were we wrong in our interpretation, nor were we kept long in the dark us to the nature ot

The first was þÿ lo what extent the system of Colonial Administration, known under the denomination ot Responsible Government, this þÿisland; and the second þÿ that system, to whatever degree it may he to have been instituted, has been since carried out in practice. þÿ 1 hese

questions, said Mr. Jordon, surprised him, as they did his colleagues; so after due deliberation, the Executive Committee strenuously repudiated kind or accountability of any responsibility degree or whatsoever. The Governor thinks otherþÿwise that they should he reasonably, and, in sound policy, answerable for the consequences >! their advice or measures to the Legislature, and that he should not be planted as a target every discontented quarter. to be fired These at oppo- from site views have kindled the elements ot political discord, brought the real business and have consequently of the country to a stand-still. the honorable gentlemen know that his Excellency the Governor desired them to recognise the principle of governing j through Parliamentary majorities branch party? Edward Jordon, who at the þÿGovernor s request, and upon his responsibility, presented a hill, of which the following is a transcript, for the consideration of the House:

þÿ A Bill in aid of the Act for the better Government of the Island (17lli Vic., cap. 29.) þÿ Whereas the occupation of seats in the Assembly by holders of offices of emoluments inconveniently restricts the selection from that body of members of the Executive Committee : Be it enacted by the Governor, Legislative Council, and Assembly of this island, and it is hereby enacted by the authority of the same, as follows : þÿ I From and after the passing of this act, any person who is the holder of an office of emol nient, except the members of the Executive Committee and the Attorney General, shall hereafter be incapable of being elected as a member of the Assembly, any other law of this Island, or section of a law, to the contrary notwithstanding. þÿ 2. lfany person hereby declared to he incapable shall nevertheless he elected and returned as a member of the House of Assembly, such election and return

intents and purposes whatsoever. þÿ 3. The consideration of Mr. þÿJordon hill s lias been postponed till Tuesday next. In the meantime, and preparatory to a decision upon the question of parliamentary responsibility, a variety of resolutions were proposed, till at length the following one of the member for Metcalfe (the Hon. Mr. W estmoreland) was carried on division by a majority of seven: þÿ þÿ That the Act of the better government of the Island affairs establishes the responsibility of the Governor for the sue- j proper 'conduct of public officers, and although the said Act may not define the responsibility of the ExecutiveCommitlce to the Legislature, the power is inherent in this House to invoke that responsibility to this House, when the occasion for its exercise may þÿarise. to invoke the responsibility of the Executive Committee to the House whenever the occasion for its exercise may arise. On Thursday evenin'; the lion. FEDERAL COERCION Some of t lie Washington correspondents telegraph that Mr. Buchanan is attempting te map out a middle course in which to steer his bark during (he tempest which now howls about him. He is to condt-mu the asserted right of Secession, but to assert in the same breath that he is opposed to keeping a State in the Union by what he calls Federal Coercion. Now we have nodesire to prevent Secession by Coercion, hut wo hold this positiou to be utterly unsupported by law or reason. Mr. Buchanan, as President, bears little or no relation to the States as States ; he is the Chief Magistrate not of any particular States, hut of the Union. His special and paramount duty is that of taking care that the laws are duly aud faithfully enforced and obeyed. Of course, South Carolina's eloquence and rhetoric, her passion and pride, her armaments and threats, are nothing to liirn so long as she refrains from any actual resistance to the Federal authorities and laws. But let her undertake to stop the running of mails through her territory, and the collection of the Federal revenues, and the case would be gravely altered. The President could know nothing of Carolina in the premises, hut he could not help dealing with violators of the laws and disturbers of, the peace. These he must overcome and bring to justice, without hesitation and without compromise. He may recommend a Convention, or a new Compromise; he may even affirm the abstract Right of Secession ; yet he has but one thing to

do þÿ respect and obey the laws himself, and call on all others to do likewise, leaving all beyond to the adjudication of the proper tribunals. There is no alternative, no ground for ambiguity or hesitation. Whatever a Convention may or may not do, the President has but one course open, and that we have just pointed out. The fact that a State has undertaken to put herself out ol the Union is nothing to him, unless he has concluded to go out with her þÿ to which oxtent we feel sure that the sanguiuo expectations of Mr. Keit 1 will not. be gratified.
