The London Athentrum says that a bit of romance about Garibaldi may help to explain the hostility of the Dictator ol the Two Sicilies to France, and that ot the Emperor of the French toward the Liberator of Italy. The family of Garibaldi, like the family of Bonaparte, is Corsican ; and the name of I'ozzo di Borgo or of Louis Blanc is evidence with what fiery hale a Corsican inav pursue his vendetta against lb.it lucxy race. The Dictator's grandfather, Joseph Baltisfa Maria Garibaldi, was one of those patriot Corsicans who gave the crown to Count Von Neuhotl, crowned Theodore the First of Corsica; and being sent by the new king Von Ncu- sage to his mother, Madam on a mesh ff, who lived at Peddenbh, near Ruggeherg, in the Mark Country (now part ol Westphalia), Garibaldi there fell in love with the king's sister, Catherina Amalia, and, with his Sovereign's consent, married her. The registry of this marriage, we read in a Rhine paper, is still to be seen at Ituggeberg. In the same year, Garibaldi took Catherina home to Ajaccio; but, fortune failing flic patriot, Theodore fled before the Genoese to England, where he became the idol and butt ofWalpole, who traduced his cha-

G- R . 0 I X A V I: S, racter and wrote the inscription over his monument in St. Anne's Church þÿ , Stuttgart can fully rival those cities. bevailing the fortune which "Bestowed a kingdom and denied him bread." Joseph Battista Maria Garibaldi fled from Corsica to Nice, where, after the French conquest and occupation of the island put an end to the last hopes of independence, he forgot politics and practiced as a physician. His grandson is the Dictator. Meanwhile the offences of the Bonapartes against the Garibaldis have grown in bulk and atrocity. Corsica has been made French. Nice has now been made French. The old country, the new country, are alike gone. More, I the very last home of t be hero is menaced. Caprcra, the lonely green rock in the Straits of Bonifacio, which he has bought with his gains and peopled with his pigs and asses, belongs to the islai d of Sardinia and must follow its path should a new " recovery" of territory to France take place. Thus, the Bonapartes seem to chase the Garibaldis j like an evil fate, leaving them no feet of earth on which the soles of their feet can rest in peace. W ho can wonder at the Dictator's doubt, suspicion, and dislike? A romantic speculation may be allowed to close the record of those romantic facts. Theodore King of Corsica, left no lawful son. An illegitimate son, known about London streets as Colonel Frederick, a man of mark in his day, pistoled himself under one of i the porches of Westminister Abbey. The title has been declared by the Cor-

sican Parliament hereditary to Theodore's family, a near branch of w hich Dictator Garibaldi now represents. Thus, Garibaldi's title to the throne of Corsica is just as good as that of Louis Napoleon was a dozen years ago to the throne of France.

(From the Illustrated London News, Dec. 1. 1860.) FRANCE. Napoleon met willi an enthusiastic reception on Monday night at the Opera No sooner was his M je-ty perceived in the Imperial box than the crowded house broke out into vehement cheering, in te-timony of what is felt by the intelligent classes rejecting the new decree. Count Flahaut is definitively appointed F rench Ambassador to the Court of St. James's, M. Momy having declined the appointment. Count Walewski has been appointed Miuister of State, in place of M. Fould, whose resignations lias been accepted. An Imperial decree confers upon M. Vintry t!u rank of Commander of the Legion of Honour. TheMoniteur of Tuesday contains the following appointments: þÿ Count Perstgny, as Minister of i lie Interior; M. Billault, as Minister without portfolio; M. Forcade Laroqu. tie, , as Minister of Finance; M Magne, as Minister without portfolio; M. Beneditti, as Councillor of State for extraordinary service. The Moniteur of yesterday week published a convention concluded between iheGoveruments of Sardinian and France, arranging several questions in reference to the annexation of Savoy and Nice. It is determined that the portion of the Sardinian debt chargeable to Savoy and Nice shall be 44 millions of Rentes, which the French Government shall remit to Sardinia. The charges incurred by Sardinia on account of Savoy aud Nice will be transferred to France. CONSTITUTIONAL REFORMS. Last Sunday's Moniteur contains one of the most important d< crees which (he official journal of France lias registered since the erection of

the second Empire. The Emperor has decided to permit the Senate aud Legislative Body more directly to participate iu the responsibility of Government. Henceforward the Chambers will freely discuss the domestic and foreign policy of the Emperor's advisers, and speeches will be reported in the newspapers. The following is the Imperial decree, which may possibly end iu changing the whole Government machin. ry of Imperialism: þÿ Napoleon, by the grace of God and the national will, Emperor of the French : to all whom these presents may concern, greeting, þÿ Wishing to give to the great bodies of the Slate a more direct participation iu the general policy of our Government, aud a striking testimony of our confidence, we have decreed, and do hereby decree, as follows: þÿ Art. 1 . The Senate and the Legislative Body shall vote every year, at the opening of the Session, an address in reply to our speech. 2. The address shall be discussed in presence of the Government Commissioners, who shall give to the Chambers all necessary explanations as to the home and foreign policy of the empire. 3. Iu order to facilitate the expression of the opinion of the Legislative Body in the making of tho laws and the exercise of the right of amendment, Art. 54 of our decree of the 22nd of March, 1852, is again put in force, and the regulation of the Legislative Body is modified in the following manner: þÿ "Immediately after the distributions of the bills, and on a day fixed by tlie President, the Legislative Body, before

naming its committee, shall hold a secret sitting, at which a summary discussion shall be opened, in which the Government Commissioners will take part. The present clause is not applicable either to bills of local interest or to cases of urgency." 4. For the purpose of rendering more prompt and more complete the reproduction of the discu-sinns ol the Senate and of the Legislative Body, the following senatus consulton shall be p. e-eiited to the filiate ; þÿ "The reports of the sitiings of the Senate and of the Legislative Body drawn up by the reporters placed under the authority of the President of each Assembly shall be sent every evening to all the journals. The debates of each sitting shall also be reproduced by shorthand writing and inserted in extenso in the official journal of the next day.'' 5. During the continuance of the Sessions the Emperor will appoint Ministers without portfolio to defend before the Chambers, in concert with the President and the members of the

Council of State, the bills brought forward by the Government. 6. The minister of our Household is suppressed, and its attributions are united to thuse of the Grand Marshal of I he Palace. 7. The Ministry of Algeria and the Colonii s is suppressed, and the Colonies are uuittd to the Ministry of Murine. 8. The services not directly connected with public instruction, or with the special establishments of the university, are removed from the Ministry of Public Instruction and placed in the attributions of the Ministry of State. 9. The service of the breeding studs is removed from the Ministry of Aericultuie and Commerce and attached to the attributions of the Ministry ofSta'e 10. Count de t'hasseloup- L ubnt, ex-Minister of Algeria and the Colonies, is named Minister of the Marine and Colonies, in the room of Admiral Hamelin, appointed to other functions. 11. Admiral H.melin is named Grand Chancellor of the Legion of Honour, in the room of Marshal Pelissier, Duke de Malaki ff, appointed to other functions. 12. Marsha! Pelissier, Duke de Malukoff, is ntitn-d Governor- General of Algeria. 13. The Ministers without portfolios have the same rank and salary as Ministei s exercising I unctions They lurm pat t of the Councils of Ministers, and have losideiiccs provided by the State. 14. Our Minister of State is charged with the execution ot this decree. Done at the Palace of the Tuilerits the 24th of November, 1860 (Signed) NAPOLEON. (Countersigned) A. WALEVVSKI.

The non-official part of the Wiener Zeilung of this day contains the following notice : þÿ " By electric telegraph we learn that there were such lamentable excesses at Debreczin, at I 7 o'clock in the evening of the 26th iust , that , military intervention was necessary. A torchlight procession in honour of Count Carolyi, the Obergespan of the Szathniar county, who was passiug through Debreczin, on his way to Szathmar, led to the excesses. Between 20 and | 30 persons were arrested. The necessary measures for preventing similar occurrences have been taken." The Vaterland of this day further states that the result of the interference of the troops was that about 20 persons were wounded, and some few (einzelnc) killed. The private information which has reached me on the subject is to the following effect : þÿ At 7 o'clock in the evening of the 26th inst., a vast crowd assembled in front of the hotel in Debreczin, and loudly cheered Count Carolyi. At a later hour þÿ probably at 9 o'clock þÿ the people went, to the County-bouse, from the front of which they pulled d.wu the Imperial arms, and trod them under foot. In the course of the evening visits were paid to almost all the Government offices in the place, and in some of them sad excesses were committed The tobacco in the Government magazines was destroyed, and the books in the taxoffice are said to have shared the same fate. No attack was made on the police-offiee at Debreczin, but every window in the house of the j

burgomaster of the place was broken. The people offered no opposition to the troops, hut many of them w ere wounded while trying to < scape from the scene of action. It is even said that a few persons were killed. The levy of lecruits is said to have been the immediate cause of the outbreak at Debreczin ; but it cannot be doubted that the movement was a revolutionary one, as thousands of voices ciied, " Long live Kossuth !" " Long live Garibaldi !" On l lie same day, and almost at the same hour, there were disturbances at Eperies, and it is to he supposed there was an understanding between the inhabitants of that town and those of Debreczin, as the same excesses were committed in both places. The troops were called out at Eperies, but I have not heard that there was any collision between them and the people. gress, or the filibustering aggrandizement of the South, from the Mexican annexations downwards, or tiro Fugitive Slave Law, or tho Dred Scott decision, or the Kansas-Nehraska Act, þÿ it is not these, or any other triumph of democratic insolence during their ascendancy of half a century, that has commanded the sympathy and admiration of Europe. TO THE EDITOR OF THE WEST INDIAN Dear Sir, þÿ I have read the correspondence of Mr. Samuel Johnson, which appeared in your number of Friday last There are various opinions on the subject of tire signature as well as the letter itself. Some urge that there are no traces of' Johnson, the Lexicographer, as the spelling and orthography generally are execrable ; others maintain that there is no trace of Ben Johnson, affirming that there is no wit, þÿtho abundance ot craft ; others say, that Brown Jones, and Robinson would have carried oil appearances equally well or, nearly so, us Samuel Johnson, Esq., with his affectionate remembrances to his Barbados friends; but the majority persist in asserting that the genuine þÿ nature would have been article of a sig- Bryan, Johnson, Humbug, & Co þÿ I am rather disposed to the last opinion. Only think what an Elysium of a place Santa Cruz must be þÿ where people have only to express a want, and it is responded to by the generous inhabitants, who pour gratis, , stranger all that is to meet his utmost de- without recompense, into the laps of a sires. This is marvellous generous, I say, Mr. Editor ; mark my word, it is marvel- : lous, generous. When you see Mr. Bryan next, look him full between Lis eyes, and ask him if þÿI m not right about this idea as to the marvellous. And only think, again, for a labourer to get Eighty Cents per day for doing nothing þÿ or that which is so near nothing, that something, þÿ even what may be called a half grown something dont re-

present it. And this is marvellous too þÿ marvellous easy way of getting Eighty Cents. If I could get yourself and a few friends to join me, perhaps I may bid my final adieu to Barbados myself, and slope to Santa Cruz. But a friend at my elbow says, you will hardly go with your freepress notions, as the Press is not free in Santa Cruz þÿ that its liberty is rather cramped, and its Editors very much ? gag- ged. O dear, Sir, can this be true Be-

. cause where the Press is not allowed liberty, I dont think the people in such a place can be so free after all. Then a few words aside. Please tell me Mr. Bryan as much as this in a corner. Tell him that Samuel Johnson had made a wretched bad imitation of the Quashey style. Ask him who ever heard of an ignorant fellow like Sam knowing any thing about inverted commas þÿ þÿ Simmonds. Tell him to omit these tell-tale scratches the next time that Sam is disposed to write ; and besides, the Capitals are rather too uniformly in place for an ignoramus like Sam. Say to him that it is so much more economical, too, to advertize Letter fashion, with 1 lie broad fist of (the feigned?) Samuel Johnson, which the Editor publishes, as the good folks of Santa Cruz supply the want of strangers, for nothing ; and so the expense ot an Advertisement is saved. And besides all this, it looks so much more natural to put! and play the game of marvellous after the fashion of a correspondence, than to be figuring after this sort in the shape of an Emigration þÿAgent s Advertisement, who is, of course, always suspected of speaking two words for number one, and only one for Santa Cruz ; but, particularly, let him know that people go marvellously too far sometimes, ami that, whoppers do not obtain generally the currency þÿ while what is called a little þÿfellow may that it is desired, slip down. This, of course, for Mr. þÿBryan s, ear. Very truly yours. VERITAS. October 16.

Despatches received at the Merþÿchants Exchange Reading Room, were the first to disseminate the news, although the extremely gratifying fact that all lives had been saved, accompanied the cai'lie.-t accounts, there was an intense anxiety manifested to learn the full particulars of the disaster, but no information could lie obtained until the anival of Captain Leitch or some of the passengers. The first despatches received were as follows: þÿ þÿ The steamer Connaught sprang a leak on Saturday last, and took fire on Sunday morning. Abandoned All hands þÿsaved. Scituatb, Oet. 2. þÿ A boat from the brig Minna Schiffer, at this port, reports that on Sunday, Oct 7, fell in with the steamer Connaught, Capt. Leitch, from Galway for Boston, and took off her passengers and crew. The brig arriving off Scuuate at an early hour yesterday, Capt. Leitch, accompanied

s e i ft 8 1 a. y i. s , by a passenger named Cox, left the vessel in a boat and took the cars for this city, where he arrived at about 11 þÿo clock. The following statement was given to, and phonographed by, oue of our reporters : þÿ Statement of C aptain l.eiteli.

The Connaught left St. þÿJohn s, N. F., on Wednesday, at fifteen minutes past two þÿo clock in the afternoon, the wind then blowing from the 8. W at a moderate rate ; this continued until Friday, when a fresh and strong breeze continued to rise from the S S YV. and W.N.W.; at this time everything on board the steamer was in the best possible condition ; at length the wind increased to a perfect gale, and continued increasing until Saturday evening; about 8 o'clock the next morning a leak was discovered in the engine-room by an engineer on duty, who immediately reported it torn..; I quickly called all hand- on deck, and issued general orders in effect that the leak should be stopped as soon as p is-ih'o The engine pumps and bilge ejections were immediately got ready, hut proving insufficient to the requirements of the occasion, all the deck pumps were forthwith rigged: shortly afterwards two pot table fire engines .vote got ready and conveyed down into the engine-room and forward stoke hole ; these were put into active seivice; at this time haling was also commenced by a portion of the crew, who were sengers; spiritedly assisted by efforts the united not a tew ot the pas- of the passcngeis and crew were kept up tor quite a time, aud not w ithout a favorable result, tor in a short time the water decreased; but this state ot affairs did not last long, for the water again began to increase, and soon flowed with great rapidity into the engine-room and forward bunkers; aud so rapidly did the leak gain on us, that we tound

it impossible to keep the vessel free ; in transacting the above, 1 suppose we were occupied about twelve hours; by eight o'clock on Sunday morning the water bad increased to such an extent that it completely extinguished the i (ire under the forward boilers; at this time passengers, yet great deal of excitement among mani- all seemed resolute aud the fested a disposition to help us all they could; to this line of conduct there were but few excepti ns; the crew quickly obeyed all my commands, and worked remarkably bard; there was some little, confusion, but the majority of those þÿht, on board kept quite þÿ decreased so much as it was impossible for silent ; the steam now any human being to keep below þÿ that the engine stopped of itselt About iiiue discovered mue and a half þÿo clock, the engineer þÿo clock, or smoke coming up fioni the alt stoke-hole, and reported the circumstance immediately tome; on his stating to me lie thought the ship was on fire, I ordeied all the force pumps and hose to be brought up on deck ; these were put in active service and used to the fullest extent ; wet blankets and all other appliances at our command were used to extinguish the lire ; buckets weie used in conveying water down to the ted; place or where we the supposed the fire a portion of passengers still continued to be locato assist, us all they could. The ladies among the cabin passengers behaved very þÿwell indeed they exhibited but little sign of fear, yet appeared as a matter of course, greatly excited. in the hold so

fast Finding that the fire increased and I set a poition of the crew passengers to pumping in, thereby compelling them to abandon the work of pumping out ; as to decreasing the smoke, this apparently proved ineffectual ; still the pumping in was continued. At this time I made preparations to save the passengers, aud ordered the boats to be got in readiness ; the þÿport boats were first got out; the first boat was stove alongside the steamer in a heavy þÿsea all the. others were successfully launched, there were three life-boats launched, ns two also þÿ þÿcutters four others, and a gig þÿ comprising þÿ At this tinm very a þÿ þÿmail-boat, few of the passengers manifested any particular desire to converse. The first boats were launched about 3 þÿo clock on Sunday þÿafternoon the the last one, in the course ot three hours afterwards. Wo hoisted three signals of distressone at each mast-head, and one at the main gaff; soon after, a man was sent aloft to make observations; " he had not been long 1 up when ho cried out, Sail on the lee bow In a few seconds afterwards another vessel was observed bearing the same way ; both vessels were stand

ing to the North ; the first, which proved to be a bark, passed on without paying any attention to or seeing our signals; the other was a brigantine ; at the time, our head was to the W.S.W.; the wind from the N W , with a very heavy sea; the brigantine bore down E.N.E., and by the time it got within hailing distance, two boats were manned and a portion of the passengers got ready to be conveyed to the brigautiue ; the first boat was a small one, and contained eight or ten persons; the other, a lifeboat, and must have held some thirty five persons; the majority of the crew of each boat was composed of women Great exertions were still being made on board the steamer to keep the fire in subjection; water in every possible shape and manner was fioe y used; every aperture that could possibly he el ised up was covered, in eider to exclude air and keep the vessel from going down ; a great number of the passengers were lower, d down into the boats by a single rope from tiie weather side of the steamer ; others were get on board from the lee side ; at first we Could not keep the boats on the La side of the steamer iu consequence of the ship drilling fast down on the boats ; but, after a while the sea somewhat moderated, and with great care we succeeded in getting the boats on the lee side of the steamer, so that they could receive the remaining passengers; the small boat referred to above was the first one tb it reached the brigantine ; the passengers were quickly and safely conveyed on the brig-

þÿantine deck, s after which the boat returned to the steamer It was only by the utmost exertion that the fire could be kept down, while the passengers were being past into the boats. On the weather side of the vessel the iron became so heated that the passengers were forced to go to the lee side of the steamer; the plates of iron commenced warping iu every direction ; the deck becaute quite warm ; indeed, so much so, tinit the heat c ,uld be felt through the soles of þÿone s s hoes ; aud what made it still more uneomforta de, the pitch commenced melting out of the seams of the spar deck ; the smoke to issue from the sky-light and companion way þÿ also fiom the engine-room, hatch, and stokehole hatches. At this time it was an utter impossibility for any one to look into the main abaft engine-room ; I now catne to the conclusion that the vessel would inevitably be burned up; at about nine þÿo clock p m the fire bioke through some portions of tiie deck, as well as through the tiist skylight ; wet blankets and the hose were brought quickly to bear, hut with only partial success. About half-past nine þÿo clockthe passengers were all placed in the boats, and soon afterward on t he deck of the brigantine; the flames could be no longer subdued ; they broke through the forward saloon skylight and deck with terrible force ; in a short time the flames extended up to the masthead, and almost instantly burnt all the mainstays and other topes, as also a sail that was set on the mainmast to keep the steamer steady.

At tiiis time a boat which had just returned from the brigantine was sent forwatd under the lee fore-tigging to get some provisions, if possible ; in short, all that could be got out ; I now sent that portion of the crew which remained, to the last boat, aud with the assistance of Mr. House, my first mate, and others, examined the ship to see no one was left on board ; it was only with the greatest difficulty that wo could do this; as the smoke and heat now became intolerable, we left the steamer and took to the boat ; when wo abandoned the steamer it was about fifteen minutes after 10 þÿo clock p. m , and when we reached the brigantine it was about. 10 30. Every attention was shewn the passengers on board the brigantine ; the captain acted in tiie most attentive manner to all alike. The last we saw of the steamer was at about three þÿo clock a. m. on Monday; then it appeared one solid mass of flame in the distance. On Sunday wo spent onr time in sitting and laying round on the decks of the brigantine. While on boaid the steamer many of the steerage passengers came to me and offered all they had to be saved; but when they got safely on board the brigantine, they appealed somewhat dissatisfied, and called for soft bread, as dry biscuits were being passed round. I think the fire originated in eonsequenco of the felt round the boiler taking fire : the fire originated at the aft boiler, on the starboard side.

The Post says most providential was the appearance of the brig Mimia Shaffcner at the period of the disaster. Had she not been at hand to render assistance, the result would have been one of the most heart-rending and fearful calamities that the sea or land lias ever witnessed, and the horrors of that wholesale destruction of human life no pen could havejustly described. arrival of the passengers at BOSTON. The brig arrived at the foot of India wharf, at one þÿo clock yesterday afternoon, under tow of the Resolute Her arrival was greeted with shouts of applause by the crowds of people who had assembled upon the wharf, and filled all available position upon neighbouring vessels. As the brig rubbed greatly against the piers, and the pushing out of a plank seenn.d to make þÿ assurance doubly þÿsure, (in regard to the safety of the unfortunates) hearty and long continued cheers went up in token of warm sympathy and hearty congratulation. 1 lie mans, the only articles saved from the Connaught , were landed, and then followed one of those emitn ntly interesting, yet, in some respects sad scenes, incidental to the arrival of a large body of emigrants. Husband greeted wife, son welcomed mother, relatives of all relations united in fo. d embrace. þÿ but, on the other hand, there was a sad view to the picture. Vain search for father, husband, son, or brother, resulting in the discovery that death had been less merciful to him, presented striking contrast to the joy with which it mingled,

and iu one instance we heard escape horn the lips of one poor woman, under whose protecting care clustered a group of bare-headed, barefooted, and ragged children, the regret that she ! had escaped a watery grave. The littleness of some, and their utter inability to decide for themselves, where first to go, or what first to do, was a feature of the scene never to be forgotten. We shall never forget it As a general thing the passengers presented a healthy appearance, þÿ as neat as could have been expected, considering the close quarters to which they had been coufined for the past forty-eight hours. Most of them appeared to be warmly clad, but among them were some women who were not, so fortunate. Some were seeking friends whom they did not know by sight, and ran up and down the wharf calling on all they met to point them out. One stout. Irish girl had nothing with her but her prayer book, which site bad clung to throughout the whole catastrophe. The aged and feeble ones, as they reached the wharf and found no acquaintances sat down despairing, not knowing where to go. The brig Minna Shiffcr belongs to New York, was from Malaga for Boston, and had on board a valuable cargo of oranges and other fruit, which, it was at first reported, were till thrown overboard, to make room for the Connaught's people ; but such was not the case It was not found necessary to dispense with the cargo, and the people from the Connaught, in addition to the limited stores saved from the ill-fated steam-

er, subsisted on the fruits aud wines with which the brig was laden, on the passage from the scene of the disaster to Boston. With the crew of the brig, when all of the þÿsteamer com- s pany were embarked in the first named vessel, she had 602 individuals within her narrow limits.

GENERAL PARTICULARS. The origin of the fire is not known with any | degree of certainty. The Chief Engineer is of opinion that it proceeded from the ignition of the heavy woollen felting with wnicli the boilers were encased. If such had been the case the fire would naturally smoulder for considerable time before breaking out. The steamer had on board ,410,000 in silver, which was sent from the Bank of Newfoundland, at St. þÿJohn s, to their agent in Boston. The specie was a total loss. The mail hags were all landed on de:k at an early stage of too disaster, and tiieieby saved The passengers behaved admirably throughout the whole affair. There was iio confusion or panic at any time, although 180 females were of tiie number of passengers One or two fell overboard from the brig, and the same occurred in the. ha-te to tuke tiie boats, which was soon cheeked, hut no lives were sacrificed. The officers and crew of the Connaught numbered 123 men, and the passengers 406, making in all 591 souls. Of the passengers 59 were

S T, CROIX # v i cabin, and the rest were composed principally of immigrants. The steamer sailed from Galway at 3 p. in on the 25th Sept., þÿ arrived at St þÿjohu on s 3rd of October. After repairing paddle floats, which were damaged on the passage, the steamer left for Boston. At, St. þÿJohu s eight passengers were landed, and ten taken on board. It is stated that there were fifteen feet of water in the hold when the fire was first discovered, aud that the vessel would, at any rate, have fouudered. The wooden boats were smashed, and to the four metallic boats were the rescued pat ties indebted for the safety of their passage to the brig It is said that the brig M. S. on Monday at 6 a. in spoke the schooner Elizabeth of Digby, N. S.. and made request that she should relieve the Minna Shiffer of a portion of the passengers. With the reply that the Elizabeth had no provisions to spare the request was declined.

At a meeting of the passengers held on board the Minna Shiffer, the following am ng other resolutions were passed : þÿ þÿ Resolved,that we tender to Captain John Wilson, to Mr. Thos II. Connaughton, arid to the crew of the brig Minna Shiffer our warmest, and most grateful thanks for their humane, noble, generous, self-sacrificing and heroic exertions in securing our deliverance from imminent death ; that we recognize them as the instruments in the hands of God of our preservation; we will ever cherish their memories in our holiest n collections, and delight to do honor to I their names in every portion of the þÿworld. Resolved, that we feel the gieatest pleasure in bearing testimony to the intrepid coolness and fidelity of Captain Leilch and his courageous officers in securing our Bafety, and contributing to our comfort, and we pay to them a heartfelt tiibute of gratitude for their untiling exertions in the appalling peril that betel þÿus. Before the meeting adjourned $500 were subscribed for a testimonial to Oapt. Wilson, of the Minna Shiffer, (who is said to he every inch a sailor), and the first officer, Thos. Connanton. The brig had only six men on hoard, four of whom were Spaniards, and two Englishmen. When the small boats of the steamer touched her side, Capt. Wilson says some of the crew of the Connaught attempted to conceal themselves among the passengers on deck, aud it was only with the greatest difficulty lie could force tlum to return to the burning vessel.

The officeis deserve the gieatest praise, hut the sailors the greatest cuudemuatioii for the cowardly manner in which they acted. Among the passengers Loin Newfoundland to Boston, was our old friend Captain Richard Meagher, toimeily of this city. Leilch, and his officers, in saving the passengers, and for his assistance to Capt. Wilson in piloting the Minna Shiffer to the port of þÿBoston. o ( From the Panama Star and Herald.)

CALLAO, Oct. 11th, 1860. Yesterday a most frightful accident occurred in the Dry Dock, at San Lorenzo, involving the entire loss of the Peruvian frigate Callao , (Auperimac) and almost the entire destruction of the dock, and a fearful loss of life. The particulars of this lamentable affair are, as far as I can gather, as follows: It having hern deemed advisable to dock the ship in order to examine her copper and other trifling things, the Engineer of the dock was asked it she could be taken on with her battery, provisions and crew on hoard ; his opinion was that the dock could not raise her with that weight, consequently her guus were landed, yards sent down and top gallant masts struck, retaining her provisions, magazine and crew on board, and in this state she entered the dock at 10J a. tn. There was a very large concourse of persons went over to witness tiie operation. The government steamer Ucayali conveyed the President, Minister of war. and a large

number of invited guests. þÿ Upon the arrival of the President the vessel began to enter the dock, and was soon placed in her proper position, the pumps were set to work, every thing up to the present moment went well. The keel of the frigate took the chocks of the platform, and she began to ascend out of the water, after some time the Engineer noticed that the after sections of the dock were rising much quicker than the forward ones, the extra weight of her anchors and chains being the cause of this As soon as the sections were agaiu level all the pumps were again started, and presently four of the upright stanchions of the dock broke þÿ this was, however, deemed of no importance, as everything else was going on well, and the frigate coming out of the water; she was now out about six feet above her hearings, her keel in the chocks (the Callao lias a deep keel and a very flat floor) but ow'iug to her great depth of keel the chocks did not act as any support whatever on her bilge, therefore the ship was simply balanced upon her keel, and so long as she could be kept steady in that position she was safe, but her crew were on boaid constantly moving from one side to the other, the ship being already tnpheavy, this caused her to give one or two slight rolls and then slits pitched over on her starboard beam ; at the second surge the three masts snapped about half way up from tie deek, her starboard ports being open, she rapidly filled with water, and here begau a scene ot horror impossible to describe.

Hie water was filled with men and women, wounded, dying, all screaming for help; boats loss o" life would have been still mere fearful. were promptly scut to their assistance, or the Of the number that were below at the time very lew escaped, and their cries lor help were terrible, but that which was most heart-rending was the pour siek iu the hospital, who, helpless with disease, could do naught hut scream for that help that none could render them. Up to the preseut time ot writing it is not known how many have been lost, but it cannot fall short of one hundred and fifty. The wounded that could be removed who did not require amputation were brought over to Callao, the rest remaining on the Island. 'The number of broken heads, .oms aud legs is great Capt. Kerr, of the English ship Golconda , lowered his boats and did good service in saving some thirty or forty lives. The Callao was a fine 44-gun trigate and was built in Bliekwall by Messrs. Green and William, aud she was a splendid specimen of naval ai cbiteotui e. þÿ She is about six years old þÿ the vessel is a total lo.-s being entirely under water, the dock may also be considered as done for, it having failed as a commercial spe- < dilation, and the present disaster may he considered as the last of the Callao Dry Dock The loss ol this vessel may have a very important effect upon the policy of Genl. Castilla þÿ he having asked the other day from Congress extraordinary powers ; this is supposed by many to mean a simultaneous declaration of war

against Ecuador and Bolivia þÿ he having got it into his head that those two nations are levying agiinst him, any how if such were his intentions he cannot carry them out at present As I wrote yon in my last letter, the mercantile houses who had been awarded the guano contracts with the government modifications would not accept them, the contracts have been altered, and there is a probability that the government will have to accede to the propositions as they were originally made, and in that case the house of Gibbs & Co. will still retain the English contract. In Bolivia the revolution is suppressed again, several guilty officers were shot: Belzu himself had never crossed the frontier. The departure of the Lancaster and Naraganselt from this place will cieate a void not easily filled. The officers of these two vessels have won golden opinions for their gentlemanly conduct and hospitality during their brief stay amongst us. If their motto had beeu peace and good will to all mankind they were indeed its faithful portrayers. Yours truly, FELIX.
